appendExercises.q: Rebuild **the one diagram**: drag each name onto its layer.
appendExercises.explain: **Spark computes. Storage persists. Delta gives stored files table semantics. Unity Catalog governs the objects.** The compute engine (Spark/Photon) reads and writes the Delta table; the Delta table (Parquet files + transaction log) physically lives in cloud storage; Unity Catalog registers it under `catalog.schema.table` and checks permissions. The control plane and the workspace are real things — but not layers of this picture.

why.compute: Compute is ephemeral: when the cluster terminates, nothing of the table lives there.
why.delta: Delta is the *format* (files + log). Those files are stored in cloud storage — that is what persists.
why.uc: Unity Catalog stores the name and permissions (metadata), not the table’s bytes.

appendExercises.q: The cluster terminates tonight. Tap the layer that still holds the table’s **bytes** tomorrow.
appendExercises.explain: **Cloud storage** (S3 / ADLS / GCS) keeps the Parquet data files and the `_delta_log`. Compute and storage have **independent lifetimes**: compute can stop, the data stays.

appendExercises.q: `SELECT * FROM main.sales.orders` — trace who gets involved, in order.
appendExercises.explain: You send SQL → the **compute engine** runs it → it resolves the name `main.sales.orders` and checks your permission in **Unity Catalog** → reads the **Delta** log to learn which files form the current snapshot → reads those Parquet files from **cloud storage**. Debugging tip: a PERMISSION_DENIED fails at the UC step; a missing file fails at the storage step.

appendExercises.q: Cover & recall the four layers. Answer each question in your head, then reveal.
appendExercises.explain: If you can name all four layers and say what each one is responsible for, you can place almost any Databricks feature or error on the right layer.

appendExercises.q: Drag the medallion layers (and the step that builds Gold) into place.
appendExercises.explain: **Bronze** = raw, source-faithful. **Silver** = cleaned, validated, deduplicated, CDC applied. **Gold** = business-shaped aggregates for a specific audience, built by an **aggregate / model** step. Medallion is a recommended *pattern* of progressively increasing quality — not a law.

why.silver: Silver is exactly what the buggy rule produced — rebuilding from it keeps the bug.
why.gold: Gold is derived from Silver: it inherited the bug.
why.pg: The source may no longer have the old data — that is why we keep Bronze.
why.kafka: Kafka retention may already have dropped those events — that is why we keep Bronze.

appendExercises.q: Your Silver rule was wrong (`amount = amount * 100`). Tap the layer you rebuild Silver **from**.
appendExercises.explain: From **Bronze**: Bronze → corrected code → rebuild Silver. That is the reason to keep raw, “dirty” data: without it you may have to re-request it from the source — and the source may not have it any more.

why.agg: This step builds Gold (aggregates) — the data is already clean by then.

appendExercises.q: All labels are hidden. Tap the step where **duplicates are removed and CDC is applied**.
appendExercises.explain: The step between **Bronze and Silver**: parse, validate, deduplicate, apply CDC, cast types. Bronze stays source-faithful; Gold only aggregates already-clean Silver data.

appendExercises.q: Trace one order change from **PostgreSQL** to the **CEO dashboard**.
appendExercises.explain: PostgreSQL → **Bronze** (raw change) → clean/dedup/CDC → **Silver** `orders` → aggregate → **Gold** `daily_sales` → dashboard. Each hop has one responsibility, which is what makes failures easy to localise.

appendExercises.q: The CI pipeline is covered. Drag its five steps into the right boxes (left → right).
appendExercises.explain: CI on every push / PR: **lint → unit tests → integration tests → configuration validation → build**. If anything fails: don’t merge, don’t deploy. Deploying to production is CD, never part of CI.

appendExercises.q: Now the CD flow: pick each step.
appendExercises.explain: CD: **main branch → tests → deploy staging → integration tests → deploy production**. Continuous *Delivery* may keep a manual approval before prod; continuous *Deployment* goes automatically. Either way: validated code → automated, controlled deployment.

why.dev: DEV is for experimenting with sample data — it does not prove prod-like permissions or configuration.
why.prod: In PROD real consumers would be hit if the check fails.

appendExercises.q: Where are permissions, dependencies and configuration checked **without** impacting real consumers?
appendExercises.explain: **TEST / STAGING**: close to production, but no real users. That is where “works in dev, fails in prod” problems (missing grants, different config) should surface.

why.depprod: Production comes only after staging and the integration tests there pass.
why.build: Build produces the artifact; it deploys nothing.
why.main: Merging to main deploys nothing by itself.

appendExercises.q: CI is green and the PR is merged. Tap the **first** step that touches a real, non-dev environment.
appendExercises.explain: **deploy staging**. Validated code goes to staging first, integration tests run there, and only then **deploy production**.

why.cp-area: The control plane schedules and coordinates — your Spark workload does not run there.
why.cp: The control plane schedules and coordinates — your Spark workload does not run there.
why.browser: Your browser only shows the notebook; it does not run the groupBy.
why.storage: Storage holds the data; it computes nothing.
why.sl-area: That is the serverless plane — this notebook is attached to CLASSIC compute.

appendExercises.q: Your notebook runs on **classic** compute. Tap where the `groupBy` actually executes.
appendExercises.explain: In the **classic compute plane**: the driver and worker VMs in **your** cloud account. The control plane (Databricks-managed) only manages and coordinates.

why.cp-area: Serverless compute is Databricks-managed too — but it is a compute plane, not the control plane.
why.cl-area: Classic compute lives in your account; on serverless you do not configure VMs.

appendExercises.q: The same notebook on **serverless** compute: tap where it runs now.
appendExercises.explain: In the **serverless compute plane**, managed by Databricks: it allocates, scales and manages the compute. The control/compute separation stays the same — only *who manages the machines* moved.

appendExercises.q: Follow one notebook command on classic compute (any worker will do for the 4th step — use the one next to storage).
appendExercises.explain: Browser → **control plane** (schedules / coordinates) → **driver** (plans the job, splits it into tasks) → **workers** (run the tasks) → **data storage** (read / write).

appendExercises.q: Which plane is which? Drag the names.
appendExercises.explain: **Control plane** (web app, APIs, orchestration, metadata) and **serverless compute** are Databricks-managed; **classic compute** (driver + worker VMs) runs in your cloud account.

regions.label: Data file (Parquet)
regions.note: Data file: the real rows, column by column (Parquet).
regions.q: What kind of file holds the real rows?

regions.label: Deletion vector
regions.note: Marks deleted rows of a data file without rewriting it.
regions.q: What marks deleted rows without rewriting the data file?

regions.label: Transaction log folder
regions.note: The versioned table state: one commit file per version (+ checkpoints).
regions.q: Which folder holds the versioned state of the table?

regions.label: Commit file (JSON)
regions.note: Commit file of version 1: JSON actions (add / remove / metadata).

regions.label: Checkpoint
regions.note: Checkpoint: a Parquet summary of the table state up to v100.

appendExercises.q: Name the parts of a Delta table.
appendExercises.explain: **Data files** (Parquet) hold the rows; **deletion vectors** mark deleted rows without rewriting a file; `_delta_log/` holds the versioned state: one **JSON commit** per version and periodic **checkpoints** (Parquet summaries). File statistics live *inside* the add actions of the log, not in a separate file.

why.j000: Replaying from v0 is exactly what the checkpoint avoids.
why.j001: Replaying from v1 is exactly what the checkpoint avoids.
why.p0: Data files are read for the query — the question is which LOG files rebuild the snapshot.

appendExercises.q: A reader needs **snapshot v103**. Tap every log file it loads to compute it.
appendExercises.explain: **checkpoint v100 + replay 101, 102, 103** — not v0 → v103. The checkpoint summarises the state up to v100. (The exact checkpoint interval is an implementation detail: never rely on it.)

why.fc: C is in the current snapshot {C, D} — VACUUM never deletes it.
why.fd: D is in the current snapshot {C, D} — VACUUM never deletes it.

appendExercises.q: After the retention period, which files can **VACUUM** physically delete?
appendExercises.explain: **A and B**: no longer referenced by the current snapshot, only by old versions. After VACUUM, time travel to those old versions stops working — that is why time travel is not a backup.

appendExercises.q: Cover & recall: what is each covered part of a Delta table?
appendExercises.explain: Data files + deletion vectors + `_delta_log` commits + checkpoints = the Delta table state.

appendExercises.q: `WHERE customer_id = 2500` — tap **every** file Delta must actually read.
appendExercises.explain: **C** (2001–3000) may contain 2500 and **D** (1–3000) may too. A and B are skipped by their min/max statistics. File D shows the pitfall: a file with a wide range can never be skipped.

appendExercises.q: `WHERE customer_id = 1500` — tap every file that must be read.
appendExercises.explain: **B** (1001–2000) and **D** (1–3000). Data skipping only reads files whose [min, max] range could contain the value.

appendExercises.q: `WHERE customer_id BETWEEN 900 AND 1100` — tap every file that must be read.
appendExercises.explain: The range overlaps **A** (…–1000), **B** (1001–…) and **D** (1–3000). Only C is skipped. Range filters across file boundaries read several files; liquid clustering keeps ranges narrow so fewer files overlap.

appendExercises.q: Uncover as few tiles as you can: what mechanism does this picture show?
appendExercises.explain: **Data skipping**: per-file min/max statistics in the Delta log let the engine skip files that cannot contain matching rows. Partition pruning works on folders/partition values — a different mechanism.

why.ljob_s: Serverless doesn’t support the custom JAR / low-level Spark this job needs.
why.lint_c: All-purpose is for interactive work; a scheduled job belongs on job compute.
why.lint_s: This is a scheduled job, not interactive work.

appendExercises.q: Example C: nightly ETL that needs a **custom Spark JAR** and low-level Spark not supported on serverless. Tap the right compute.
appendExercises.explain: Automated + classic required → **Classic Jobs compute** — then you choose DBR, workers, autoscaling, access mode, Photon.

why.lint_c: Not an all-purpose cluster: BI/SQL traffic belongs on a SQL warehouse.
why.lsql_p: Possible — but serverless is the recommended default for BI today.
why.lsql_c: Possible — but serverless is the recommended default for BI today.

appendExercises.q: Example D: **100 analysts** query from **Power BI**. Tap the best default.
appendExercises.explain: SQL / BI → SQL warehouse → usually **Serverless SQL warehouse** (recommended today for BI, SQL ETL and exploratory analytics).

why.lint_s: Serverless notebooks don’t support **R** (nor Scala/RDD APIs per the source).
why.ljob_c: You want a notebook to work in interactively, not a scheduled job.

appendExercises.q: Example E: you need an **R notebook**.
appendExercises.explain: Interactive + a feature serverless doesn’t support → **classic all-purpose** compute (possibly Dedicated access mode).

appendExercises.q: The first question is “what is my workload?”. Drag the four workload types onto the branches.
appendExercises.explain: **Interactive**, **Job**, **Pipeline**, **SQL/BI** — then choose serverless or classic. Streaming is not a separate branch: it runs as a job or a pipeline.

appendExercises.q: Name the five layers of the compute stack.
appendExercises.explain: Top to bottom: **your workload → execution engine (Spark JVM / Photon) → runtime (DBR) → compute nodes (driver + workers, VM shapes) → infrastructure (classic / serverless)**. Governance (Unity Catalog) is not a compute layer.

why.row-infra: Classic vs serverless is about who manages the machines, not their shape.
why.row-runtime: The runtime is the software environment, not the VM.

appendExercises.q: You choose `r5d.4xlarge` for the workers. Tap the layer that choice lives on.
appendExercises.explain: **Compute nodes**: driver type and worker type are VM shapes. DBR, Photon, node types and serverless are not alternatives on one level — each has its own layer.

why.row-engine: Photon/Spark is the engine; the DBR version is the environment it ships in.
why.row-nodes: The VM stays the same — the software on it changes.

appendExercises.q: You upgrade **DBR 15.4 LTS → 16.4 LTS**. Tap the layer that changes.
appendExercises.explain: The **runtime**: the versioned environment (Spark + Python + JVM + libraries). The same code in a different runtime can behave differently — that is why versions and LTS matter.

regions.label: Workload
regions.note: What you write.

regions.label: Execution engine
regions.note: What executes the plan: Spark (JVM) and/or the vectorized Photon engine.

regions.label: Runtime
regions.note: The versioned environment (DBR, LTS, ML) your code runs in.

regions.label: Compute nodes
regions.note: Driver type and worker type = VM shapes; autoscaling changes the worker count.

regions.label: Infrastructure
regions.note: Who manages the machines: you (classic) or Databricks (serverless).

appendExercises.q: Hard mode: type the name of each layer.
appendExercises.explain: Workload → Execution engine → Runtime → Compute nodes → Infrastructure. Place every new term (Photon, LTS, pools, autoscaling…) on one of these layers.

regions.label: Driver
regions.note: Builds the plan, splits it into stages and tasks, schedules them, tracks executors. Does not process the partitions.

regions.label: Worker node (VM)
regions.note: A worker VM. In Databricks classic: one executor per worker.

regions.label: Executor
regions.note: The JVM process that runs tasks — one per worker.

regions.label: Core = task slot
regions.note: One active task per core.

regions.label: Local disk
regions.note: Shuffle files and spill are written here — gone when the VM goes.

appendExercises.q: Drag the names onto the cluster.
appendExercises.explain: The **driver** plans and schedules; each **worker** VM runs **one executor** (Databricks classic); each **core** is one task slot; the **local disk** holds shuffle files and spill.

why.e1: Executors run tasks; they don’t build the plan.
why.e2: Executors run tasks; they don’t build the plan.
why.e3: Executors run tasks; they don’t build the plan.
why.e4: Executors run tasks; they don’t build the plan.

appendExercises.q: Labels hidden. Who builds the plan and schedules the tasks?
appendExercises.explain: The **driver**: SparkSession, logical → optimized → physical plan, stages and tasks, scheduling, tracking executors. It does not process the partitions itself.

why.driver: Spill happens on the workers that run the tasks, not on the driver.

appendExercises.q: A big sort **spills**. Labels hidden — tap where the spilled data goes.
appendExercises.explain: To the **local disk of the worker** running the task (as are shuffle files). Spill is not a failure, but heavy spill is slow; and local disk content vanishes with the VM.

appendExercises.q: Uncover as few tiles as you can: how many tasks can this cluster run **at the same time**?
appendExercises.explain: 4 workers × 8 cores = **32 task slots** (the driver is excluded). A stage of 100 tasks therefore needs ≈ ⌈100 ÷ 32⌉ = **4 waves**.

appendExercises.q: The boxes are shuffled. Tap the **first six** phases in dependency order.
appendExercises.explain: **Compute → Delta Lake → Unity Catalog → Ingestion → Structured Streaming → Declarative Pipelines.** Each layer needs the previous one — unlike the workspace menu order.

appendExercises.q: Now the end of the road: tap phases **6 → 10** in order.
appendExercises.explain: **Declarative Pipelines → Jobs → Databricks SQL → Performance & Debugging → Production CI/CD.**

why.p2: Delta commands themselves run as Spark tasks on compute — so compute comes first.

appendExercises.q: Every MERGE, OPTIMIZE or streaming write finally runs as tasks on … tap it.
appendExercises.explain: **Compute**: to reason about why a MERGE is slow or why a write creates small files you first need cores, task slots, partitions, shuffle and memory.

appendExercises.q: Which phase treats storage, namespace, governance, identities and permissions as **one system**?
appendExercises.explain: **Unity Catalog** (phase 3).

regions.label: Metastore
regions.note: Top-level regional UC container for metadata and permissions.

regions.label: Catalog
regions.note: Catalog: the primary unit of data isolation.

regions.label: Schema
regions.note: Schema: a finer organisational / access-control layer inside a catalog.

regions.label: Table
regions.note: An object registered in prod.silver: a table.

regions.label: Volume
regions.note: An object registered in prod.silver: a volume.

regions.label: Function
regions.note: An object registered in prod.silver: a function.

appendExercises.q: What kind of thing is each covered box?
appendExercises.explain: **Metastore** (regional top container) → **catalog** → **schema** → objects (**table**, **volume**, **function**…). The workspace is not a level of this hierarchy.

why.metastore: The metastore is the regional top container — you don’t create one per project.
why.sbronze: Schemas are a finer organisational / access-control layer.
why.ssilver: Schemas are a finer organisational / access-control layer.
why.sgold: Schemas are a finer organisational / access-control layer.

appendExercises.q: Tap the **primary unit of data isolation**.
appendExercises.explain: The **catalog**. Isolation usually starts at catalog level (dev / prod / sandbox); the schema is a finer layer; the metastore is regional.

appendExercises.q: Which of these is **not** part of the namespace `catalog.schema.object`?
appendExercises.explain: The **workspace**. A notebook *lives in* a workspace; `prod.silver.orders` is *registered in* the metastore. “Workspace above catalog” is wrong.

appendExercises.q: Resolve `prod.silver.orders`: tap from the top container down to the object.
appendExercises.explain: Metastore → catalog **prod** → schema **silver** → table **orders**. To read it you need USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA + SELECT along this same path.

why.schemaloc: schemaLocation keeps the schema history — not progress. Exam questions swap them on purpose.
why.bronze: The table has the rows, but not the stream’s progress.

appendExercises.q: The cluster died after files A and B. Where does the restarted stream learn that A and B are done?
appendExercises.explain: The **checkpointLocation** stores progress (files processed, offsets, batch ids). On restart it reads the checkpoint and processes only C.

why.ckpt: The checkpoint stores progress, not the inferred schema.

appendExercises.q: Where are the inferred schema and its evolution (`_schemas/`) kept?
appendExercises.explain: Under **cloudFiles.schemaLocation** (set on the read). Pointing both options at one directory is allowed — the two *roles* stay different.

appendExercises.q: Pick the name of every piece of the Auto Loader skeleton.
appendExercises.explain: Landing zone → **Auto Loader** (`readStream.format("cloudFiles")`) → **writeStream** (Delta) → **Bronze table**; state: **schemaLocation** (shape) and **checkpointLocation** (progress).

appendExercises.q: Cover & recall the moving parts.
appendExercises.explain: Read side: Auto Loader + schemaLocation. Write side: writeStream + checkpointLocation. Commit to Delta first, then advance the checkpoint.

appendExercises.q: Max event time seen = 10:20, watermark delay **5 min**. Tap the point on the axis where the watermark is.
appendExercises.explain: Watermark ≈ max event time seen − delay = 10:20 − 5 min = **10:15**. It follows event-time progress, not the wall clock.

why.e17: 10:17 is newer than the 10:15 watermark → still accepted.
why.e19: 10:19 is newer than the 10:15 watermark → still accepted.

appendExercises.q: Delay **5 min**. Tap every arriving event that **may be dropped** as too late.
appendExercises.explain: Watermark = 10:15. **10:03 and 10:12** are older → may be dropped (“may”, not “will”). 10:17 and 10:19 are accepted and update their windows.

appendExercises.q: Same stream, but the delay is **20 minutes**. Tap the watermark now.
appendExercises.explain: 10:20 − 20 min = **10:00**: all four events are accepted — at the price of more state, bigger checkpoints and higher latency.

appendExercises.q: Fill in the checkpoint folder.
appendExercises.explain: **offsets/** (what each micro-batch reads), **commits/** (which batches were written), **state/** (stateful operators) and **metadata** (query identity). A checkpoint is not just a “last timestamp”.

why.offsets: offsets/ = what each batch READS — not whether it was written.

appendExercises.q: Spark must know whether micro-batch 42 was **written to the sink**. Which entry tells it?
appendExercises.explain: **commits/** — the record of micro-batches successfully committed to the sink, a key part of exactly-once.
